section_title: When Following Jesus Divides a Family

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 34 Do not assume that I have come to bring peace to the earth; I have not come to bring peace, but a sword. 35 For I have come to turn ‘a man against his father, a daughter against her mother, a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law. 36 A man’s enemies will be the members of his own household.’

37 Anyone who loves his father or mother more than Me is not worthy of Me; anyone who loves his son or daughter more than Me is not worthy of Me; 38 and anyone who does not take up his cross and follow Me is not worthy of Me. 39 Whoever finds his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for My sake will find it.

context_lines: Jesus now describes the division His coming can bring, even within a household. The sword image explains conflict around allegiance to Him. It belongs with the earlier warning about family betrayal in [Matthew 10:21](https://biblehub.com/bsb/matthew/10.htm), and should be read alongside His instruction to love enemies in [Matthew 5:43–48](https://biblehub.com/bsb/matthew/5.htm). The disciples are being prepared to face opposition, rather than commanded to attack their families.

His words about divided households draw from [Micah 7:5–7](https://biblehub.com/bsb/micah/7.htm), where betrayal reaches close relationships and the prophet turns in hope to God. Jesus uses that language to describe how deeply the response to Him can divide people.

The issue in verse 37 is loving family more than Him. He names parents and children, the strongest of ordinary bonds, and calls for loyalty to Him even when those claims compete. The saying is not a judgment that family love itself has no value; its force lies in the greater claim He makes.

Taking up a cross deepens the cost. Following Him may mean surrendering security and even life. The final contrast is between trying to preserve life at the cost of allegiance to Him and losing life for His sake. The promise is that life given to Him is not finally lost.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians commonly understand these sayings as requiring loyalty to Jesus above competing loyalties and willingness to share the cost of following Him. [Wesley on Matthew 10:34–39](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-gospel-according-to-st-matthew/) explains the divisions through opposition to the gospel and the cross through faithfulness when avoiding hardship would mean doing wrong, while the Catholic [Catechism, 520](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P1L.HTM), presents Christ's own humility and hardships as the example His disciples follow.
god_plan_lines: The disciple's cross belongs within Jesus' own path. In [Matthew 16:21–27](https://biblehub.com/bsb/matthew/16.htm), He speaks of His coming suffering, death, and resurrection, then again calls His followers to take up their cross. The call is shaped by the Savior who goes before them.

[Philippians 2:5–11](https://biblehub.com/bsb/philippians/2.htm) joins His willing service and death on a cross with His exaltation by the Father. God's saving purpose moves through self-giving toward life and glory. Following Jesus means placing one's life with that Savior, whose own suffering was not the end of His story.
